inventory.name: Permissions-Policy: focus-without-user-activation — policy-controlled feature controlling programmatic focus in frames without user activation

syntax.rationale: The declaration surface is the policy directive and its controlled operation set defined in #syntax: when denied for a browsing context, programmatic focus operations are blocked unless triggered by an active user gesture. The section details the affected operations with semantic <code> elements: element.focus() scripted focus calls on any element, window.focus() requests to self or child windows, the autofocus attribute on form controls on load, dialog.showModal() automatic focus, and popover auto-focusing of interactive children, while explicitly preserving user-initiated focus.

inputs.rationale: #examples documents the declarative configuration syntax and parameters: the HTTP response header directive Permissions-Policy: focus-without-user-activation=() denying all subframes or focus-without-user-activation=(self) allowing top-level while restricting subframes, and the iframe element allow attribute syntax allow="focus-without-user-activation 'none'" or allow="focus-without-user-activation 'src'". It also documents JavaScript capability detection via document.featurePolicy.allowsFeature('focus-without-user-activation').

outputs.rationale: The observable output of denying the policy is silent no-op enforcement: programmatic focus calls in denied contexts are ignored without moving document focus and without throwing exceptions. The section also specifies the delegation exception output: an embedder frame holding focus can programmatically pass focus into a child iframe regardless of child policy denial, after which the child may navigate focus internally.

errors.rationale: The permissions policy mechanism defines no throwing surface, DOMException, or error event: programmatic focus calls under policy denial fail silently by specification design to avoid breaking existing scripts or leaking cross-origin embed states. FLAGGED GAP: no DOM error or event is exposed to script; Chromium logs a debug console message when focus movement is blocked, but this is a developer diagnostic rather than a script error interface.

context.rationale: #at-a-glance defines the execution and exposure environment: Origin trial in Chrome 149–151 (stable ship targeted for 150), governed by WHATWG HTML PR #10672, the W3C WebAppSec Permissions Policy explainer, and ChromeStatus feature 5179186249465856. Applicable to top-level and embedded browsing contexts via HTTP header or iframe attribute.

lifecycle.rationale: #syntax documents the activation state lifecycle: programmatic focus is restricted while the browsing context has no transient user activation; upon receiving genuine user activation (direct clicking or keyboard tabbing), the restriction is temporarily lifted for the current task. Additionally, focus delegation governs transition into child frames: once a parent delegates focus into a child iframe, the child context gains focus and can move focus within its own subtree.

examples.rationale: #examples provides four complete, semantic <pre><code> code blocks: (1) HTTP response header denying all iframes (Permissions-Policy: focus-without-user-activation=()), (2) iframe allow attributes explicitly denying third-party embeds ('none') while allowing trusted first-party frames ('src'), (3) HTTP header restricting subframes to self (Permissions-Policy: focus-without-user-activation=(self)), and (4) JavaScript feature detection querying document.featurePolicy.allowsFeature('focus-without-user-activation').

compatibility.rationale: #compatibility provides a browser support table detailing Chrome (Origin trial 149–151; stable ship targeting 150), Edge (Tracking Chromium), Firefox (No signal as of Chrome 149), and Safari (No signal as of Chrome 149), citing ChromeStatus feature 5179186249465856 and blink-dev. Note: ChromeStatus record discrepancies regarding Safari's view ('Support') and origin trial endpoint (milestone 152) are reported as divergences in notes.

securityPrivacy.rationale: #why-it-exists provides an extensive security and privacy rationale: third-party embedded content (ads, widgets, comments) running in nested browsing contexts can programmatically call element.focus() to silently steal focus from top-level user interactions. This allows malicious embeds to intercept keystrokes by focusing hidden text inputs, suppress parent keyboard shortcuts, or disrupt form submissions. The focus-without-user-activation policy gives embedders declarative control to prevent cross-frame input snooping and focus hijacking.

(2) ORIGIN TRIAL ENDPOINT: this page reports 'Chrome 149–151', while ChromeStatus record stage 150 lists desktop_last, android_last, and webview_last as milestone 152 for trial BlockingFocusWithoutUserActivation. (3) SHIP MILESTONE AND STATUS: this page reports 'Expected stable ship' as 'Chrome 150', while ChromeStatus record reports browsers.chrome.status.text as 'In developer trial (Behind a flag)' and leaves stage 160 shipping milestones null. (4) FLAG NAME: this page names generic experimental flag chrome://flags/#enable-experimental-web-platform-features, while ChromeStatus record specifies dedicated flag_name 'blocking-focus-without-user-activation'. (5) DEFAULT ALLOWLIST: this page states 'The default allowlist for focus-without-user-activation is * (all frames allowed)', while the WHATWG HTML Living Standard (§2.2 Policy-controlled features) defines focus-without-user-activation with a default allowlist of 'self'.
